---
title: "Exploring proteins"
---

After [differential abundance analysis](differential-abundance.html), look more
closely at individual results. Here we follow ISG20 through its sample quantities,
precursor profiles, and supporting peptide identifications in the HepG2 DIA demo.

```{r setup, include=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ProteoVaultR)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
    dev.args = list(bg = "white")
)
sample_info <- tibble::tribble(
    ~sample_name,   ~sample_id, ~condition,
    "Control_R1",  "Ctrl1",    "Control",
    "Control_R2",  "Ctrl2",    "Control",
    "Control_R3",  "Ctrl3",    "Control",
    "IFNa_12h_R1", "IFNa1",    "IFNa",
    "IFNa_12h_R2", "IFNa2",    "IFNa",
    "IFNa_12h_R3", "IFNa3",    "IFNa"
)
sample_info$condition <- factor(
    sample_info$condition, levels = c("Control", "IFNa")
)
```

## 1. Choose a protein

Reopen the database and attach `sample_info` from
[Preparing data](preparing-data.html). Use the exact `source_group_id` from
`fit$results` to select a protein group:

```{r select-protein}
data_dir <- Sys.getenv("PROTEOVAULTR_DEMO_DIR", unset = "demo-data")
vault <- open_vault(file.path(data_dir, "hepg2_ifna-dia.proteovault.duckdb"))
vault <- set_sample_metadata(vault, sample_info)
protein <- "sp|Q96AZ6|ISG20_HUMAN"
protein
```

ISG20 is a single-protein group in this demo, so the same identifier also selects
its sequence. For a group with several members, select an individual member's
accession for the coverage plot.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Stored quantities:** These plots read the database. Any additional normalization
or imputation you applied to `se` stays in that R object.
:::

## 2. Compare sample quantities

```{r protein-abundance, fig.alt="ISG20 protein-group quantities across three control and three IFNa-treated HepG2 samples."}
plot_protein_abundance(vault, protein)
```

ISG20 has higher recorded abundance in all three IFNa samples. Check whether a
change is consistent across replicates when reviewing your own results.

## 3. Inspect precursor profiles

Look at the precursor measurements associated with the group. This demo stores
precursor quantities in `matrix`, so select that method:

```{r precursor-profiles, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, fig.alt="Log2 quantity profiles for the modified peptide and charge-state precursors associated with ISG20."}
plot_protein_precursor_quantity_lineplot(vault, protein, method = "matrix")
```

Each line represents a modified peptide and charge state. Profiles measured in
both conditions generally increase in IFNa, agreeing with the group-level result.
Only positive quantities are drawn; lines can span missing samples, so check the
points as well. The x-axis lists independent replicates, grouped by condition.

## 4. Examine sequence coverage

Map validated peptide identifications onto the stored protein sequence:

```{r sequence-coverage, fig.width=9, fig.height=7, fig.alt="ISG20 sequence coverage from validated peptide identifications, shown separately for each sample with observed modifications marked."}
plot_protein_coverage(vault, protein)
```

Each sequence row has a coverage strip for every sample. The subtitle pools
coverage across samples, while the sample labels report their individual coverage.
Markers show observed modifications. Use this view to inspect supporting
identifications alongside the quantity plots.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Peptide specificity:** A uniquely placed peptide matches one position within
this sequence. Peptides shared with other proteins can still contribute to
coverage, so consider protein-group membership when interpreting the plot.
:::

Close the connection when you have finished:

```{r close-vault}
close_vault(vault)
vault
```
